identifications.body:
The first thing that caught my attention is that this beetle has the spot pattern of 1,3,4 instead of 2,3,4. In layman's terms, the front pair of spots are way too far forward and this is not a variable trait by any means.

It also has a bold dark central suture. At first I thought it was just the wings slightly parted (revealing the black abdomen), but that does not look to be the case.

You would be forgiven for thinking it was C7 though!

comments.body: Thank you! I had been wondering if those differently sized side/back spots were somewhat consistent among individuals, very cool and good to know.

@awenninger Nice find.  Thanks for asking for clarification.  We can all learn from it.  I didn't know about this species.   @silver_starsong Thanks for the detailed information.  It would be nice if these kind of descriptions were included in INAT.  It would certainly help with identifying.  I've looked at the photos on bug guide link for Johnson's, just wanted to confirm the head and pronotum look the same as a Seven Spotted Lady Beetle?  Thanks.
As far as I know the head and pronotum are the same as seven-spotted, yeah.

@silversea_starsong Thanks.    On this particular observation, the forefront spot seems to be more forward than on the typical Seven Spotted Lady Beetle where it's set back a little further. For my identification purposes, do you know if the forefront spot can be this far forward for Seven Spotted Lady Beetle?  In my identifications, I have observed that some Seven Spotted Lady Beetles have extra spots or markings this far foward.  I'm wondering if there's another species I may not know about.  I want to make sure I'm identifying the lady beetles correctly.  Thanks.

This was what I was referring to above with the forward spot being the tiniest or reduced in European species. None of the markings have changed positions, but the forward marking in seven-spotted has been reduced to a smudge and is barely visible. You can see it fairly well here:

https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/47898535

identifications.body: Dark central suture, and different markings. In the American species, the side spot is the tiniest and the backmost marking is a bundle of two spots, whereas in the European species the frontmost spot is the tiniest and the others are all larger single spots.

comments.body:
It's not really a subspecies, at least not that is certainly known. Certain regions have spotted ones, others have spotless ones. Specific Channel Islands offshore are also split this way with only one or the other.

Nonetheless this is a very good find, they seem to have almost disappeared from the coastal south.
Wow, a spotted California ladybug. Didn’t know this subspecies existed!
